item.title: Conscious Intelligence Is the Key to a Fulfilled Life
item.description:
Intelligence

Conscious Intelligence Is the Key to a Fulfilled Life

Consciousness connects the mind with life.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Consciousness arises when life begins to feel itself.
  • A fulfilling life cannot grow from disconnection between life and mind.
  • Cultivating conscious intelligence is the greatest gift to our lives.
The emergence of conscious intelligence in life
Source: Fermin Rodriguez Penelas / Unsplash

This contribution continues my exploration of the experience of a fulfilled life, or a life worth living. Here, I would like to explain in more detail why consciousness plays a central role in this, and why caring for our consciousness—or conscious intelligence—should be a top human priority.

Following a lifetime of empirical research into the relationship between the body and the nervous system, Antonio and Hanna Damasio demonstrate how consciousness emerges from the regulation of life through homeostatic sensations. Consciousness is the connection between life and the mind (Damasio, 2026).

This is remarkable because the disconnection of the human mind from life has deep historical roots in our culture and continues unabated. This is the strange order of the modern world. It seems to me that a fulfilled life cannot arise from this ancient wound of disconnection between life, the mind, and consciousness.

When Life Feels Itself

What strikes me particularly about Antonio and Hanna Damasio’s work is that they do not describe consciousness as something that hovers above life, but rather as something that emerges from it. Consciousness does not appear first and then accompany life. Rather, life itself begins to feel itself (Damasio A. & Damasio H., 2020, 2022, 2023, 2024).

Homeostasis, or the continuous regulation of the organism, provides the basis for existential feelings, which then act as a bridge between body and mind.

From this perspective, the idea that a fulfilling life cannot be achieved through the separation of mind and life takes on profound significance. If consciousness is rooted in life, then alienation from life becomes more than just a cultural or psychological issue. Instead, straying from our living selves undermines our very sense of fulfillment.

When the Mind Disconnects

Modern humans have gained unprecedented control over the world. However, they have also lost much of their direct participation in life. We no longer view nature as our home. We analyze and conceptualize our feelings more than we experience them directly. We categorize and polarize our human relationships more than we are present in them.

Perhaps our ancient wound lies in a gradual shift of our attention away from the living processes that sustain us, rather than in a lack of knowledge.

If that is true, then this statement becomes surprisingly sharp: A fulfilled life cannot arise from the disconnection of life and mind. This seems like a homeostatic truth. An organism cannot sustainably regulate itself when it no longer perceives the signals of its own condition. At the individual level, this leads to disconnection. Collectively, we see the same dynamic at work in burnout, polarization, ecological destruction, and the relentless acceleration of economies that absorb all our attention.

When Consciousness Takes Care of Itself

That is why I propose the following: Consciousness should be at the top of the human agenda. More precisely, we should foster the conditions from which consciousness can flourish. After all, we cannot directly create consciousness itself. However, we can foster circumstances that support consciousness, such as meaningful relationships, connection with nature, peace and tolerance, physical presence, beauty, intergenerational care, and rituals that remind us of our place in the greater tapestry of life.

In those moments, consciousness does not seem to grow through more thinking, but through a deeper participation in life itself. Perhaps that is the deepest lesson we can learn from Damasio’s empirical research. Consciousness is not merely the crown of life. It is the way in which life experiences, safeguards, and directs itself.

How Do We Protect Our Consciousness?

If that’s true, then perhaps the 21st century’s primary question isn’t: How do we create smarter systems? Rather, it is: How do we protect our ability to experience life?

This is a psychological, cultural, ethical, and perhaps even evolutionary challenge. A society that loses touch with the sources of its consciousness ultimately risks losing its humanity.

If consciousness arises from the connection between our body’s life-regulating functions and our mind, then forgetting or neglecting that relationship is the deepest form of self-sabotage.

When we look at world news, this is what we see every day. What kind of decisions does a leader make who neglects this connection? What agenda does a society have when it speaks in the name of a dogma or ideology detached from life?

And What If Intelligence Without Consciousness Takes Over?

Human culture has evolved over millennia through the regulation of life. Can intelligence, lacking sufficient awareness of life, begin to undermine itself? This is the question of our time. Cultivating awareness does not require an investment fund.

It begins each time anew with a simple act of paying attention to the life already present within us: Consider the heart that never stops beating in our chest, the pulsations of our bloodstream, and the ceaseless movement of our lungs. The quality of the flow of water and oxygen in nature is the foundation of this living body. If our mind neglects or loses its connection to life, life cannot be fulfilling.

This makes cultivating awareness the most democratic and perhaps the most revolutionary human practice. It is a nonviolent revolution that can silently change everything. This is perhaps why the cultivation of awareness should be at the top of the human agenda, as a gift to the evolution of life. This transformation creates a new evolutionary possibility: life can survive and participate in its own fulfillment. This is the gift of our conscious intelligence: It is the key to a healthy mind and a fulfilled life (De Vleeschauwer, 2026).

item.title: Identity After Retirement: Meeting Your Best Self
item.description:
Aging

Identity After Retirement: Meeting Your Best Self

How to embark on a new chapter in life as you—only better

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Retirement includes components of social interaction, independence, and identity rebuilding.
  • Retirement involves transitioning identity and the search for a new sense of meaning.
  • New roles such as mentorship can increase a sense of competence and self-worth.
  • New social contacts facilitate new identity building.

For many working people, career choice involves both income and identity. Many employees have worked within a single industry most of their lives, others have remained with the same company. Over time, particularly for employees who experience fulfillment and pride in what they do, occupation becomes identity. The personal investment in one’s choice of career enhances occupational commitment and concept of self. Yet when retirement day arrives, many employees feel lost, unsettled, and surprisingly anxious. Preparing to leave a career where someone has spent so much of their life leads them to ask, “What now?” Thankfully, there are ways to prepare for a soft landing—and for the next adventure.

Source: Image by StockSnap from Pixabay

After the Retirement Party: Same Individual, New Life

Anastasia Fadeeva et al. (2025) studied the factors that impact the transition from working to retirement.[i] Focusing on positive adaptation and adjustment, the research team examined a number of retired adults ranging in age from 58 to 82, having worked in both manual and non-manual occupations, seeking to learn the key components of success.

Fadeeva et al. found retirement includes three core components: social interaction, independence, and identity rebuilding. Of the three, one that is commonly cited by recent retirees seeking to find their place in the post-retirement world, is identity.

When Industry Is Identity

Fadeeva et al. note that a number of their participants experienced feeling a loss of identity after leaving their role at work, consistent with the reality that retirement is linked with transitioning identity and the search for a new sense of meaning. Retirees attempt to fill the gap with new roles and activities, highlight the importance of other areas of their lives, or revive previous interests or habits. Yet as we all know, new activities do not necessarily provide new meaning, and may not be consistent with one’s former, professional identity. Fortunately, Fadeeva et al. found some methods to facilitate identity reconstruction and promote a successful adaptation to retirement.

Social Identity Sustains the Test of Time

Fadeeva et al. report one of the major drawbacks cited by their study participants was loss of social relationships—a sphere that had previously defined personal or social identity. Accordingly, they note that positive retirement adjustment includes maintaining or re-establishing new social connections to provide emotional support as well as a sense of belonging and connectedness. Whether through joining a retirement association within one's field of choice, a local book club, or a sporting club, building new identity in areas of personal interest can enhance both engagement and enjoyment of post-retirement roles and activities.

Identity Through Investment—in the Lives of Others

Another area of identity development post-employment can involve a mentorship role, investing into the lives of younger people, or those new to the industry. Fadeeva et al. note the desire to become involved in the lives of others is consistent with the need for relatedness, wanting to have a positive impact on younger people for example, which could strengthen generational social bonding, a feeling of participation in society, and a higher sense of self-esteem within older adults.

New Identity Through New Roles

Another interesting finding Fadeeva et al. reported in their research, contrary to prior findings that high-quality social relationships are a basis for self-worth and competence, is that other roles provided a sense of mastery and achievement even when they did not include meaningful relationships. Thus, whether or not one has quality social relationships or maintains the same set of friends they had when working, taking on new roles or activities can apparently provide an increased sense of competence and self-worth, which increases enjoyment in retirement.

Considering all of the emotional and situational changes retirement brings, identity crisis does not need to be among them. Planning ahead to fill newfound free time is a pre-retirement activity that can be strategized with friends, family, and professional retirement planners. Proactively researching new plans and adventures, as well as ways to share a career’s worth of knowledge with others, will help retirees create a new identity—themselves, only wiser and better.

item.title: Assessing the Role of Hope for Music Therapy in Kansas City
item.description:
Therapy

Assessing the Role of Hope for Music Therapy in Kansas City

A KC therapist combines music and psychology to improve outcomes.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Music has unique capacities to access profound physical and emotional depths in service of patient recovery.
  • Dr. Wilson augments her music therapy by drawing on positive psychology concepts, especially the role of hope.
  • Her research explores the link between music and psychology to improve rehabilitation with music therapy.

Kansas City holds a special place in my heart. Four summers ago, my wife and I embarked on a road trip from New England to travel scenic byways and, ultimately, to explore the national parks of Montana and Wyoming.

Kansas City is called the City of Fountains due to its vast collection of water fountains
Source: Roy Harryman / Pixabay

On our return journey, Kansas City served as the sole urban destination of our itinerary. Among its many attributes, the city boasts a lively jazz scene—a legacy local lore attributes to Kansas City’s reputedly lax enforcement of Prohibition-era liquor laws.

About a year later, we met our future daughter-in-law and learned that her mother grew up in Kansas City. As a result, when my wife and I planned another road trip last autumn—this time through the Midwest—we eagerly included the City of Fountains1 on our route once again.

It was during the second visit to KC that I met Rebecca Lepping, Ph.D., whose work I featured in a prior post.2 When we met, Dr. Lepping introduced me to her friend and colleague, Amy Wilson, a board-certified music therapist who has since earned her Ph.D.

Wilson’s doctoral thesis investigated the use of music therapy to improve respiratory function in patients suffering from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The primary objectives of her singing intervention were to enhance phrase length (the number of syllables a participant could sing in a single breath) and pitch jumps (how big a musical interval a participant could achieve between successive notes). As a secondary goal, she aimed to leverage music therapy techniques to alleviate anxiety as a means of further improving respiratory control. In addition, she embedded assessments of hope, her personal research focus, in the protocol. Dr. Wilson emphasized that this highly interdisciplinary research was conducted alongside a team comprising a physician, a neuroscientist, and a biomedical engineer.

Dr. Wilson works at Saint Luke’s Rehabilitation Institute, a 60-bed acute rehabilitation facility within the expansive St. Luke’s Health System of the Kansas City metropolitan region. She primarily works with people who are recovering from strokes; individuals recovering from Guillain-Barré syndrome constitute another sizable component of her patient caseload. She regularly collaborates with speech, occupational, and physical therapists. Her music therapy sessions are typically conducted on a one-on-one basis, although she sometimes facilitates group singing sessions as part of patient rehabilitation.

By design, Dr. Wilson aims to harness the unique therapeutic properties of music in her practice. For instance, when treating neurological conditions that impair sensory perception, she introduces drums or chimes, utilizing tactile and auditory vibrations to help patients recover sensory function.

Beyond her clinical practice, Dr. Wilson is an active researcher. Her particular focus is the connection between music and psychology—specifically, the concept of hope. She and a colleague (Stephanie Kolakowsky-Hayner, Ph.D., CBIST, FACRM, and Saint Luke’s neuroscience research director) received a grant from the American Music Therapy Association for their research project. Titled “Recovery Through Intervention and Sound Engagement (RISE),” it marks the first funded research initiative at the Saint Luke’s Rehabilitation Institute.

The RISE study protocol calls for Dr. Wilson to conduct four individual sessions with each participant. Matching a patient’s mood with specific musical characteristics, she aims to guide each participant toward a more regulated emotional state. Mood and progress will be evaluated using a standardized hope scale that has been validated across multiple academic studies.

“Participants will choose one song that’s meaningful to them from a [curated] list,” Dr. Wilson explained to me. “They’ll identify specific goals for therapy, steps towards those goals, and then we will create a short song together. Hope is cognitive and emotional. As we use the participant’s own words in song creation, they are practicing agency in their recovery and simultaneously exercising cognition and speech. Participants will play percussion instruments to address fine motor skills, coordination, and attention.”

Dr. Wilson traces her academic interest in the role of hope in rehabilitation to her undergraduate studies at the University of Kansas. Her professor’s mentor was C.R. Snyder (1944–2006), whose seminal book, The Psychology of Hope, is widely considered foundational to the field of positive psychology. Snyder defined hope as a cognitive process rather than a mere feeling. This process, which relies heavily on the prefrontal cortex, requires setting goals, planning to achieve those goals, and the agency to pursue them. Another profound influence on positive psychology in general, and Dr. Wilson’s thinking in particular, is Viktor Frankl,3 whose work posits that hope is driven by one’s ability to find meaning in life.

Dr. Wilson is abundantly optimistic about the RISE study. She believes it has the potential to reshape how music therapy is integrated into rehabilitation, given music’s unique capacity to access profound physical and emotional depths in service of patient recovery.

“Music is a helpful tool in neurologic rehabilitation because of the way music is stored and processed in the brain,” Amy says. “By engaging in live music-based interventions, patients activate neuroplasticity, process emotions, and experience agency.”4
